description: Videos per interest with conversational learning cards. Each card has subtitle, body (2-4 short paragraphs), and takeaway.

videos.title: Will AI Take Your Job in the Next 10 Years? Wrong Question
videos.creator: Vinciane Beauchene
videos.description: Vinciane Beauchene argues that asking whether AI will take your job misses the more important question of how work itself is transforming and what capabilities remain uniquely valuable. The talk demonstrates that AI typically automates specific tasks within jobs rather than eliminating entire occupations, meaning most jobs will evolve rather than disappear. By examining cases like radiology where AI augmentation improved outcomes and increased demand rather than replacing workers, Beauchene shows that framing technology as augmentation rather than replacement leads to better outcomes. The talk emphasizes that the real challenge isn't technological displacement but ensuring workers have support for developing new skills as routine tasks automate and human judgment, creativity, and interpersonal capabilities become the primary differentiators in the labor market.

videos.title: The AI Revolution: The Future of Jobs
videos.creator: ColdFusion
videos.description: ColdFusion provides historical context for the current AI revolution by examining how previous waves of automation affected employment, showing that while specific jobs disappeared, overall employment increased as new industries and roles emerged. The video analyzes which jobs are most vulnerable to AI automation based on task characteristics rather than industry, demonstrating that routine cognitive work faces more disruption than physical labor or creative tasks. By comparing the current AI transformation to previous technological revolutions like electrification and computerization, ColdFusion reveals patterns in how economies adapt to disruptive technology while acknowledging that the speed of change this time may require more intentional policy responses to prevent widespread displacement and inequality during the transition period.

cards.title: AI Transforms Jobs, Rarely Eliminates Them Completely
cards.subtitle: Your job won't vanish. Forty percent of it might automate. The rest changes.
body: Job displacement fears often miss critical nuance about how automation works. AI targets specific tasks within jobs rather than entire occupations wholesale.
Most jobs are bundles of diverse tasks. Some are automatable; others remain stubbornly human. Your job will likely evolve—not disappear.
cards.takeaway: Think in terms of tasks, not whole jobs.

cards.title: The Right Question Is 'What Work Remains Valuable?'
cards.subtitle: You asked if your job survives. Ask what human capabilities machines can't replicate.
body: Framing the AI question as job survival creates a defensive mindset focused on preserving the status quo. A more productive approach asks what human capabilities become more valuable as routine work automates.

Creativity, empathy, ethical judgment, strategic thinking, and interpersonal connection are skills that machines struggle to replicate—and that increase in relative importance as AI handles routine tasks.
cards.takeaway: Focus on what humans do best, not what might be lost.

cards.title: Augmentation Beats Replacement
cards.subtitle: Radiologists feared AI would replace them. AI augmented their accuracy. Demand increased.
body: The radiology case study demonstrates how AI can multiply human capability rather than substitute for it. When AI assists radiologists in detecting anomalies, diagnostic accuracy improves.
That increases trust in radiology and drives higher volume of imaging studies. Better quality expands the market rather than shrinking the workforce.
cards.takeaway: AI can grow your field instead of shrinking it.

cards.title: New Jobs Emerge Around AI
cards.subtitle: Five years ago, 'prompt engineer' didn't exist. Now it's a six-figure career.
body: Every technology wave creates entirely new job categories that didn't previously exist. AI has spawned roles like prompt engineers, AI trainers, ethics consultants, and model auditors—all six-figure careers that were inconceivable five years ago.
Job creation from new technology is diffuse and gradual, making it less visible than the concentrated and immediate destruction of existing roles.
cards.takeaway: New roles emerge even as old ones shift.

cards.title: Skills Half-Life Is Collapsing
cards.subtitle: Your technical skills were relevant for ten years. Now they're obsolete in three.
body: The pace of technological change means technical skills now depreciate much faster than in previous generations. What used to remain relevant for a decade might become obsolete in three years as tools, frameworks, and best practices evolve.
This acceleration makes continuous learning a survival requirement rather than optional career enhancement.
cards.takeaway: Lifelong learning is no longer optional.

cards.title: Human Skills Become Premium
cards.subtitle: AI does analysis. You provide judgment. Judgment is increasingly valuable.
body: As AI handles more technical execution and analysis, uniquely human capabilities become the primary differentiators in the job market.
Emotional intelligence, ethical reasoning, creative problem-solving, and contextual judgment are skills that machines struggle with—and that become relatively more valuable as routine tasks automate.
cards.takeaway: The human parts of your work are becoming the premium parts.

cards.title: Transition Support Determines Social Impact
cards.subtitle: AI displaced workers. Some retrained successfully. Some didn't. Support infrastructure determines outcomes.
body: While technological change itself is inevitable, the social outcomes depend entirely on support infrastructure. Workers displaced by AI need access to retraining programs, income support during transitions, affordable education, and career guidance.
Countries with robust safety nets and education systems see workers successfully transition to new roles. Those without support see concentrated hardship and growing inequality.
cards.takeaway: Policy and support shape who benefits from change.

cards.title: Inequality Risk Is Real Without Intervention
cards.subtitle: AI-skilled workers thrived. Others fell behind. The gap widened. Policy matters.
body: Left to market forces alone, AI benefits concentrate heavily among workers with access to education, capital, and resources. Those who can leverage AI tools see dramatic productivity gains and income increases.
Those without access or skills fall further behind. Natural market dynamics widen rather than close this gap, as early advantages compound over time.
cards.takeaway: Without intervention, AI can widen inequality.

cards.title: Reframe Fear as Opportunity
cards.subtitle: You feared obsolescence. Your competitor learned AI tools. They 10x'd their productivity.
body: Fear of AI-driven obsolescence often creates paralysis precisely when active learning would provide the most protection. Workers who embrace AI tools as augmentation gain massive productivity advantages over those who resist out of fear.
The competitor who learned to use AI effectively might produce ten times the output, making their role more valuable while resistant workers become comparatively less productive.

cards.title: Purpose-Driven Work Matters More
cards.subtitle: Routine tasks automate. You ask: what's the work that matters? Meaning becomes central.
body: As automation handles routine tasks that historically filled workdays, workers face deeper questions about what work is meaningful. When you're freed from data entry, scheduling, and basic analysis, you're forced to ask what contribution matters to you and others.
Purpose and fulfillment shift from peripheral concerns to central considerations in career decisions.
cards.takeaway: Automation pushes us toward work that matters.

cards.title: Organizations Must Reskill, Not Replace
cards.subtitle: Companies that retrain existing workers retain institutional knowledge. Those that hire new AI talent lose it.
body: Organizations face a choice when AI changes skill requirements: invest in reskilling existing employees or replace them with workers who already have AI skills.

Companies that choose reskilling preserve institutional knowledge, organizational culture, established relationships, and tacit understanding that takes years to develop. Those that replace lose all of that.
